utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Unless there are any short additional observations after the Status Conference of yesterday -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're standing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. Very briefly, we have to raise a procedural issue regarding the documents which were passed on to us through the Prosecution sometime during the night and which have to do with the examination of a witness who is to be heard very shortly. It's Mr. van Lynden. We don't know whether we should discuss that now or before the witness comes. At your convenience, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and we'll see whether we deal with it now or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. Thank you, Mr. President. Again, this is becoming a strategy that is unacceptable for the Defence, of translations which arrived only a few hours ago, and it is impossible to work under those conditions. So I would like to make an oral request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to your Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that. I think we'll have to discuss it among the Judges. At the same time, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I invited all the parties to let me know yesterday whether they are missing whatever translations or documents. I didn't hear from you at that time, and I must assume that you had a copy in English of this statement and not the translation you need. And I do understand you need it, but I would have preferred to have been informed about it when we asked to be informed about it, and I think we arranged the procedure where the parties would, one week in advance, at least, compare whether all the documents are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are quite right to say that, but I don't see how I could inform you when I received these translations during the night, between today and yesterday, after our Status Conference, so I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if there was any document failing, as far as I understand. You did not have the translation in due time, so it must have been missing when I asked you. But we'll deal with it at another moment, and I'd like the Prosecution to prepare for an explanation why this was not provided earlier. Then I think at this moment the examination-in-chief of Mr. Sehbajraktarevic could continue. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sehbajraktarevic. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Extremely well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made yesterday, and it's now Mr. Stamp who will continue examining you. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were records kept of the burials done by the funeral home?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precise records, and these exist to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, typically, at what stage of the funeral process would the records be made?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wouldn't bury the dead or the killed until somebody came to report the name, the date. There were only three cases with unknown identity. We assumed they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, were those records, or copies of those records, handed over to staff from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed things over to the security forces, because I had very accurate records which I kept. I worked there throughout the war, and I gave it to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did these records indicate whether the deceased were members of the military or part of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the very beginning, not the military. The defence of the country. There was no army. There was the Territorial Defence. And after the first victims fell, the eight who were killed on the mountains above the city, I thought it wouldn't last long, so I introduced the special notebook, which is the same as a civilian one, with all the particulars being entered. I filled in one, two, three, and there were -- there was a total of 3.500 men on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you know where the records are today?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it at Bakije, in the funeral institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you handed over copies, accurate copies, of those records to the security services; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, about how many people did you bury in an average year?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And which areas did your funeral home service prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was the centre of Bosnia, and whoever was treated in Sarajevo and died there, we would drive the deceased to various towns in Bosnia, even outside Bosnia, even to Macedonia. There were quite a number of Albanians. So in fact, the whole of Yugoslavia was covered, if people died in Sarajevo and we would drive them to their place of birth, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, approximately how many bodies did you bury throughout the war, particularly between August, 1992, to September, 1994? Or I beg your pardon, particularly between September, 1992, to August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly. I could tell you roughly: 8.000 to 9.000, because the overall total by the end of the war was 13.000 people died.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just explain to me, did you mean 13.000 people died or did you bury 13.000 people?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We buried them, according to the documents that we still have, that is in safekeeping. I have the records for the period before the war, for each individual year. As I said, there was 1.000, on an average.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is when you said 13.000 people died during the war, do you mean that your funeral home was responsible for the burial of 13.000 people?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not responsible. We had to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand. Now, which areas did you service during the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipalities of Stari Grad, Centar, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad with the exception of Dobrinja, which was under siege for several months until the road was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those municipalities that you mentioned, those were the municipalities within the confrontation lines of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on average, can you recall about approximately how many bodies you buried on any given day during the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The average was about 15 funerals. That was the average but sometimes there would be five and sometimes 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you know if there were Muslim burials throughout the war apart from the ones that were carried out by your funeral home?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These municipalities, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that Dobrinja was under siege for several months. Did you manage to conduct funerals for persons from Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later, when we could reach it. Of course, in spite of all difficulties, you'd go there, pick up the body, and come back, and then you'd tell the family that the funeral would be on such-and-such a day. Those that were buried in Dobrinja, in parks and various other places, we exhumed later about 50 per cent of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how many funeral homes were operating in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pokop enterprise, which is the municipal enterprise founded by the Assembly at the time, and us. But Pokop didn't have any vehicles. The Municipal Assembly gave them one only towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there funeral homes that conducted funeral rites for Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what they did before the war. They did everything except the Muslims and the atheists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how were you notified to pick up bodies for burial?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either a family member comes, or you happen to pass by in a vehicle, or the police reports it, or the military later on, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how did you pick up the victims?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a vehicle, and we would just risk it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You risked what?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, risking whether the driver would come back alive or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the danger that the driver faced?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was danger. As you passed along the Titova Street, you had the protection of the buildings on either side. As soon as you reach Marin Dvor, it's all over. Grbavica, there are snipers that can hit you from any side. At the beginning, from the Marsal Tito barracks, there was an enormous amount of fire. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. So I take it that you mean there was a danger of snipers.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Snipers and shells. The barracks was full of snipers. They had sandbags and they would watch from behind them. They had a good overview. By then the telephones were working and the ambulance service would tell us to come, and we didn't know how to reach them. And then we'd go round about -- the roundabout way behind the railway station and we'd pick up 10 to 15 people. We didn't even know the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, how -- or may I put it this way: During the war, where did you bury the victims?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the old cemeteries of Sarajevo were dug up again, and they were protected by the buildings. The only danger was from the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you make any changes in the nature and the length of the burial rites during the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We shortened the rites to a bare minimum, just the basics. You have to bathe a man in our religion, except for soldiers. A civilian has to be bathed, wrapped up in a sheet, and then have a funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In respect to the rites at the burial place, were there any changes in the length of the ceremony during the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Non-stop, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by "non-stop, day and night"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rite itself is always the same, only it was shortened. There weren't so many prayers. But the way we worked, the transport, digging of the graves themselves, we would dig them during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did you dig them during the night?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except those two cases of the Budakovici. I've forgotten now the name. Fatima Karcic, I think her name was. At her funeral, a shell fell. It was about 4.00 p.m. A shell fell, hit the plum tree, and killed eight people on the spot. They died later in hospital. My men went there to pick up the bodies, and that is how I know. And then the Municipal Assembly gave me orders to do it at night, though it was better to do that at night, but it was much quieter at night and much safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it you mean it was better for you to bury the bodies at night because it was safer?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can't see anything. Sarajevo was in darkness, and then you would be safe. You don't switch on the light in the car either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, this funeral which you speak of which was shelled, resulting in eight deaths, do you remember what year that funeral took place?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should know the exact date. In 1993. Was it June or -- I could inquire. I have the date in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was in 1993, around June?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that. It was in the summer, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you just tell me the name of the place where that funeral was?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Budakovici. It's near the hospital, beneath the hospital, a large cemetery which we have had to dig up entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that there was sniping at your vehicles from the Marsal Tito barracks. At the time of these snipings, which party in the conflict was in control of these barracks?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers of the Yugoslav Army, the Yugoslav Army. In the military hospital upstairs, they were shooting, and also those inside. What was the name of that general? I think he came from Voyvodina. I used to know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you notice any emotional or psychological effects resulting from the shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We weren't there. Could you please just tell us, so we could record what you noticed, tell us what you observed about the emotional state of the people as a result of shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, you would hide, you would run, left and right. You'd try and seek shelter. But later on, you became indifferent as to whether you got hit or not. As soon as the shelling stopped, people would come out into the street. It's like madness. Everything was disturbed. Nothing was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you notice any changes that these emotional effects had on the population over time?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, to tell you the truth. I didn't notice these things. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I just took care of my work. I didn't have time for these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about you personally? Is there anything today that inspires any emotions about the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't even aware of what was happening. I get frightened now thinking about it, wondering how we survived, both me and my family. There were six hits. Three came from a cannon, and three, I don't know what you call them, I never served in the army, also 84 millimetres or something, shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These six hits that you speak of were where?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One in the roof, one in the balcony and two right through the building. Who they were targeting, I don't know. Maybe there is a -- there was a singer living next to me. Maybe they were trying to target him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. I take it that the building you speak of was your home?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my family home. My grandfather's, it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Finally, is there anything today that can take you back or remind you of that time when your home was shelled and your vehicles were sniped at?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately, I've forgotten all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sehbajraktarevic. That concludes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Ms. Pilipovic, you may cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your -- the testimony yesterday, when asked by my learned friends, you said where your company, the Bakije company, was located and you said that it was at Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what street?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the former Milosa Obilica Street, and it is now called Safetbega Basagica Street. There is the mosque, and then we are right by, near the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your building was shelled?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: August, 1992, until when the post office was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you said before August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can check it out. I'm not quite sure when the post office was hit, but that's when it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in the building when this happened?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It happened during the night, but all the windows were cracked, the glass shattered, the vehicles were bullet-ridden. It was -- came from about 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did a team of experts come to ascertain what had happened and was a record of the event made?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Bakije?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the building.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the post office?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, your building, the building that was shelled.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. Nobody knew -- nobody had time to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the authorities, the police, for example, that your building had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could see it. Everybody knew that. People would come there to bury people every day. Everybody knew about it. They came to bury their people every day. They said the -- it was on the news that the post office at Bascarsija had been hit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers around your building?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Today, asked by my learned friend, you said that the areas of Stari Grad, Centar, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, and later on Dobrinja, were municipalities where your company, Bakije, buried people. You said that these areas were within the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what confrontation lines they were, what kind?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see them? Were you up at the front lines, the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just went to below the line in 1992. After that, we didn't have to go there. We went to the places that were safer, and then we would bring the bodies up to Bakije. Soldiers would carry down their dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you mean when you say "subline"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the line, I mean. The line's up here, we are down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean when you say "we"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defenders, the people who could come down to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what you mean when you say "we, the defenders"? What do you mean when you say "we, the defenders"?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defenders of the city, and I was a member of one of the services.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Whose service?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The service of those defenders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were those defenders at set positions, and did you see them?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I would see them, not up at the lines but in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, no. For two years, I'm quite sure they didn't have any uniforms, and later I saw some of them in uniforms, except their leaders who would walk about town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them for the -- the president of the municipality and Stjepan Kljujic for the first time in 1992 wearing uniforms, camouflage uniforms. I didn't know they had them. I knew the olive-green grey uniforms, but that was the first time I saw people in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the weather was fine, so it must have been summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see the other people?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which other people?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The defenders.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, when they were killed. They would come in wearing tracksuits, jeans. They were children, they were young people, most of them very young.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of these, as you call them, branitelji, defenders, did you see them with weapons at all, ever?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when they would go up the hill. Every fifth person would have a rifle and they would go past my house. I would see those people. Every fifth person would have a rifle and probably a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your own house located?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the Alifakovac cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What district of Sarajevo is that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Stari Grad district, Alikovac, right there. My house is 50 metres away from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your house was shelled six times?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, six times, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was it shelled the first time?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time in 1992, when it started. One of the first shells hit the roof of my house, and the terrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see -- were you in the house when the shell hit?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the direction the shell was coming from?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know that? Nobody could keep track of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the other five times? Did you see where the shell -- did you see the shell coming?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just saw what it had done. It had shattered the roof. I would say that it came from Grbavica. But that wasn't a shell; it was a gun, from a gun, fired from a gun. And the second time was on the roof as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the gun?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I couldn't see the gun. I didn't do my military service. I'm just saying "guns," you know. I don't know what type they were. People who did their military service know about things like that. My sons did their military service, so they might know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you say you never saw the gun that you say targeted your house?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never saw it. Or perhaps I did see it but didn't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You knew it was a gun because other people told you it was?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Near your house -- were the confrontation lines near your house?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They were much further off, further up, in fact. Perhaps 30 minutes on foot you would need to reach that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What place?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at the lines?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was below the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "below the lines," that means what? What do you mean? What are you comparing it to? Below what?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean nearer town, nearer the house rather than up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where you were, as you say, below the line, were there any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they would change places. Some of them would go off and other people would replace them. There was a centre feed and then they would go up to Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to those people?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. I would say, "How are you?" "What's happening?" "Anybody hit?" Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know which military unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed it was the brigade. What was its name? He was killed later on. Kljujic, I think, the 10th Brigade. That was the one that catered to our region. I think that's what it was, but you can ask people from the army. They will be able to answer you better.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was sniping from the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1992, until the army withdrew from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When in 1992? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know. I just remember that there was this General. He was from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I passed by very quickly in a car once to save my own skin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said there was shooting from the army hospital.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, from the roof. The army was still in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself see the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that, yes. Marin Dvor they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anybody target the hospital at that time?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I watched it on television, and you could see it quite clearly, that part of Marin Dvor, quite clearly from my own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you just said that this was from Trebevic. Was it the foot of Mount Trebevic or higher up?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't really see it from where we are. You can see Vidikovac and the slope towards Vrace. At Vidikovac there was a tank. I saw that. And they shot. I saw the tank shoot quite clearly, but where it shot at, I don't know. And as to the guns, I really can't say where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every year. It happened every year. It was very noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw the tank fire, did you inform anybody that there was a tank up at Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody knew that. You could see it, you could hear it. You could hear the shell whizzing past.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo - and you said that your company was located in the centre of town - did you ever happen to see a tank in town?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the town of Sarajevo? No, I never saw a tank in the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see armed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Yugoslav army while it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Up until when?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while the barracks was there, the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that a large number of soldiers and officers were killed in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that when the army withdrew from the barracks, that the army was shot at and that more than 20 soldiers and officers were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not a soldier. Those are military matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the Budakovici case, you said that was in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure the date has been recorded and the name and surname of the woman killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you said you didn't see that personally, that happen personally.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, afterwards, I went to see what had happened when they were carrying down the dead, and that's why I'm testifying as to that. As to the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see where the shell came from?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't. How would I know? It fell from the sky. It's not a plane. It doesn't go slowly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict in Sarajevo, did you ever see a Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear that anybody had issued an order for the shelling of the Budakovici cemetery?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the shell came from, the one that hit Budakovici cemetery?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know that? No, I don't. Of course I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you just heard about that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that it had fallen and killed the people, and I took them off to hospital and then buried them the next day, two to begin with, three later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the shell falling, actually falling?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just saw what happened, the consequences of that hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told where the shell had come from?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would I care? I didn't even ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know where that particular shell came from. In respect to the Budakovici cemetery, do you know whether the confrontation lines were close by?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Spicasta Stijena was there. It's very well known. But that's quite a way off too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You mentioned Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that infamous or -- famous or infamous Spica, because lots of people were killed there, whole families, killed by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see that the interpreters seem to be a bit lost. Could the witness please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Of course, I have some difficulties, since I cannot follow the original language, so I'm grateful for that. Mr. Sehbajraktarevic, could you please look at the screen in front of you and only start answering the question once the text does not move any more, because the interpreters need some time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I know. It's English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So as soon as it stops moving, please then answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that it was the famous or infamous Spicasta Stijena. Why was it well known? What was it known by?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict, were you ever up there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear what you said, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you mean, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there might have been three snipers there, but it was fairly well hidden. What was going on behind it, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were up there at Spicasta Stijena, who were you with?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to see a carpenter whose child had been killed. He lives three houses away from the stijena, and I asked him how he managed to get to his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the confrontation lines were up there?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's none of my business. I really don't know. Nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you kept records.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were up there at Spicasta Stijena, you said you were visiting the carpenter. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were waiting for things to calm down and then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Had the carpenter lost a family member?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his son. He was 17 or 18. And then I had to go, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say where his son had been killed?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In front of his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far is the house from Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said: three or four houses away. It's not my part, it's not where I live, but three or four houses away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How many metres or kilometres is it from Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. A hundred metres, 50, 60 metres. Like this, like the door over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness a map for him to indicate the exact location of Spicasta Stijena. The map's number is 3544A, the map which has no markings. I should like to ask the witness to indicate, to mark on the map where Spicasta Stijena is and the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, could you please, Ms. Pilipovic, in view of Rule 90(H), explain to us, because this is not covered by the examination-in-chief. I do not see at this moment, but please tell me if I'm mistaken, whether this has got to do anything with the reliability of the witness. And if not, the third option might be that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes to what, Ms. Pilipovic? You say yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness, during his testimony, and in response to my questions, spoke about the confrontation lines, and it was within that framework, that is to say, the existence of confrontation lines, that I asked him what happened with the Budakovici cemetery. He said it was shelled. He said he knew the confrontation lines, and I asked him whether the confrontation lines were close to the cemetery. And then the witness went on to mention the landmark, Spicasta Stijena, or sharp rock. And to test his credibility, I asked the witness to mark on the map, because he knows where Spicasta Stijena is and he was there, where it was located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Underneath Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, would you tell us where it was, what particular location below Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence feels that this is relevant because the witness had been speaking about the confrontation lines and the existence of shelling, instances of shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first just check what exactly the witness said about confrontation lines in relation to Spicasta Stijena. One moment, please. Could you please follow me, Ms. Pilipovic? It's on my laptop computer and there is a slight difference in time. 9:48:54, the witness has told this Court, a few lines before, "I went to see a carpenter whose child had been killed. He lives three houses away from Stijena and I asked him how he managed to get to his house." "Did you see any soldiers there," was the next question. "No, you couldn't see that." And your question was, "Do you know that the confrontation lines were up there?" And the answer was, "I don't know. It's none of my business. I really don't know. Nothing to do with me." So I think if you want the witness to point at the place, either the house of the carpenter, and you would like to bring this into relation with the witness's knowledge of confrontation lines, I will not allow you to do this because the witness has testified that he had no knowledge of these confrontation lines. And when I look at the screen, you explained to this Court that the relevance of the question was that - and I'm literally quoting - "It is relevant because the witness has been speaking about the confrontation lines and the existence of shelling instances, of shelling and sniping." So if you want to test the reliability of this witness on confrontation lines, I cannot allow you to do so because he has said he knew nothing about it. If there is any other relevant issue, please explain to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness also said during his testimony with respect to Spicasta Stijena said, "the famous Spicasta Stijena." Now I'm going to ask him now why he used the word "famous."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you asked him already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Parla family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the line where he said this so we can check it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't find the line on the screen now but he said, "the famous Spicasta Stijena."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check that. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could assist, on the English text, I think it is page 19, line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is my friend referring to the English text?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying at 9.00, 47.42 minutes and seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think your laptop has a different time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 9.47?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about "famous Spicasta Stijena" I've got it on 9.47, where I read, "You've told us that it was the famous or infamous Spicasta Stijena. Why was it well known? What was it known by?" And the answer was, "The sniper." I don't know whether there was any other place where "famous" was --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could assist, because I have the LiveNote in front of me, on page 19 at line 23 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. 19, 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You will see the first reference by the witness to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "That famous or infamous Spica, because lots of people were killed there, whole families killed by snipers." That's what it says in the English translation. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question will be as follows: Does the witness have knowledge of, and if so, how does he come to know that that Spicasta Stijena was well known by the evil things that happened?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Parla family was -- all the members were killed. Maybe one member survived. He was out in the garden tending to his plot of land and they hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to visit the family?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but he's close by to the carpenter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far were they away from that spot?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first, right next door.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30 metres. They were neighbours and they could hear each other speak when people would come up to Sarajevo -- from Sarajevo. The new shift is coming shortly, and then you can do the digging.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You just said, "Others are coming to the line." Could you explain that a bit?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new shift, the people coming from Serbia for the weekend, they were the worst. That was when the shelling and shooting was the worst. Then the neighbours would let us know, and they'd say, "We won't be here so look out."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard it from soldiers who were up there talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our soldiers, those who were up there in trenches.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in that part, near the Spicasta Stijena, that there were soldiers there, that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The citizens, these Parla family, they would exchange words with them. They would communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that close to this Parla family house were soldiers that they spoke to?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were up there on that rock, and they would let them know when they should look out, and then they came out and got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They were having those conversations with soldiers near Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on Spicasta Stijena, and they were below them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So it was so close that they could talk to each other?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you kept records of the persons you buried.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How did you note down the particulars of the deceased person?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what actually particulars you noted down in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and last names, the year of birth, the name of the father, the mother, the wife, if he had one, the place of birth, year of birth, address, place where he was killed, and place where he's buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you have all that -- those data in your possession?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you provide them to anyone, if you did, to look at?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have those books, and I won't give them to anyone, but I gave a computer tape to the Security Services Centre. They copied it and returned it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by the CSB, the Centre of the Security Service?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the police. That's the name of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has been served by the Prosecution a document, D30000754, and on that disk, there is a list of victims from 1992 to 1996. That is the names of the people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who were buried by the Bakije funeral parlour. From that disk, we have copied some information, and I have sufficient copies for my learned friends opposite, for Your Honours and the witness, simply for the witness to look at this document and see whether this information has been copied from the information he gave to the police and if he could explain to us a certain detail from this table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may show it to the witness and, Mr. Usher, could you please take the copies? That would be -- you intend to tender it into evidence, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall first ask the witness whether this data come from the records he kept. We would like him to identify the document first.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is Kobilja Glava here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The document consists of 402 pages.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter "C" stands for civilian, and the letter "B" for soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So that is how you kept your records?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For me, a soldier was someone when he showed me that he belonged to the Territorial Defence, so I made a very clear distinction, and I kept the document for each of the soldier that the responsible authority, whether it was the municipality or the commander, they issued these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So in your records, you know exactly how many civilians were buried and how many soldiers were buried?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your recollection, your best recollection, could you tell us how many soldiers were buried?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you allow me to interfere, the Registrar just indicates to me that there has been distributed two different pages, so we are not just talking about one, but you gave to the registry one, and I will read the first number on the left, top corner, one indicating 00776, but another one 07233, which bears a line at the bottom, page 2. The other one I just mentioned, so the 00776 one, bears page 1. Could you please indicate and perhaps have the list being put on the ELMO? You told us that you distribute one page, and we are now confronted with two different pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has prepared, in sufficient copies -- could you just give me the beginning of the number 00 -- let me just check, 00776?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one which bears page 1 at the bottom, and the Registry has also been provided with another page, but do I understand here now you're cross-examining the witness on page 1, left, top corner, 00776?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Page 00776.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll ask the usher to get this page 2 and return it to the -- to Ms. Pilipovic. I would highly appreciate a high degree of precision on these kind of matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm doing my best but the conditions under which we are working are rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So here where it says "Status," that the letter "C" stands for a civilian and the letter "B" for combatant.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A defence member.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, for the period from 1992, from September 1992 until August 1992, how many, in your estimate, if you're able - if not, of course, you don't know - how many were soldiers and how many were civilians? And can this be seen from your records?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for that period, but from the beginning, from April 1992 until the Dayton Agreements, we buried about three and a half thousand soldiers, and the rest were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You're telling us that the data -- or do you claim that the data entered in your book have been faithfully copied on the floppy disk which was taken from you from the CSB?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't take it from me. They asked for it and I gave it to them, and they returned to me the book. That is the greatest good fortune in this general misfortune. I have all the notebooks in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the floppy disk to compare the two?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. What could they have done? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign anywhere that what they printed off the floppy disk is identical to what you have in the original?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I was just -- I just received it from them after they had finished with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So as far as I understand, everything that was in your notebook you copied on a floppy disk?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I kept my notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that everything that is entered in your book of records of the buried has been copied onto the floppy disk?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Defence, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document, Your Honours, as Defence Exhibit D27. Your Honour, my colleague tells me that it is not clear from the transcript how many were soldiers and how many were civilians among the buried. May I ask the witness this question once again to tell us how many soldiers were buried and how many civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the answer has been given as far as soldiers are concerned, and earlier in his testimony the witness answered the question on how many people in total were buried. So I think the transcript gives us no problem, but if there's any translation problem ... But of course, if you'd like him to make the totalling of numbers, which of course is quite obvious, that -- I think he talked about 13.000. If you say three and a half of them were soldiers, I would guess that 9.500 would be civilians. But if you want to ask him, of course, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you said that there were three and a half thousand soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know exactly, but about three and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in your estimate, how many civilians were buried?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine, nine and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the particulars of those nine and a half thousand civilians as to the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I remembered, I put down "shell" in my notebook. So it's not complete regarding the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't have complete information for civilians?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you abide by what you said, that you buried people from outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And during the war?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if he happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also bury civilians who were not -- who had no injuries?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If a person -- did you have proof for that person, a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have our own doctor, Dr. Zvornik [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Not Dr. Zvornik. I'm correcting -- the interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did your doctor establish the cause of death for each person that you buried, in writing, stating the cause of death, whether it was natural causes or violent causes?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take note of that in your records?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is the doctor's note in the records regarding the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was that doctor working throughout in your company?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us the name of that doctor?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Faruk Sokolovic. He's still employed at Bakije.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions, but we would like to tender an excerpt from this floppy disk, the paper beginning with 00776, the printout, be tendered as a Defence Exhibit, as the witness has identified it and confirmed that under the heading "Status," they entered an indication as to whether the buried person was a civilian or a soldiers. That is page 1, beginning with the number 00776, indicated in the left-hand corner. And in the right-hand corner, we see the words "Kobilja Glava."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Any of the colleagues at this moment -- any questions? Yes, please, Judge Elmahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: Witness, if possible, could you please specify for me whether you indeed said, in reply to a question, and I quote: [In English] "You said there was shooting from the army hospital." [Interpretation] And your answer was: [In English] "Yes, I did see that." [Interpretation] The army hospital, who controlled it and who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, it was under the control of the Yugoslav army and General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ELMAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness would like to add something or -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those days, we had access to the military hospital, and they were very fair in their treatment, and we managed to transport quite a large number of people who died there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. -- I have difficulties in pronouncing your name. Mr. Sehbajraktarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have another question in relation to the list that just has been given to you. I see different entries on that list, and Ms. Pilipovic has asked you a question about status, "C" or "B." I see that left from the column indicating status, it says "spol." I have no translation. Perhaps the interpreter could translate the word "spol" for me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Sex," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "M," "male," male or female.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Male or female. And then the last column is "mjesto."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Place," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreter tells us that that is "place." Could you please indicate to us what this place indicates. Is that the place where the person was buried or whatever other place?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Place of burial. Place of burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You just told us that you indicated sometimes also, at least not in detail, but some information about the cause of death. Would that information appear on this list as well, or is it registered somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the notebooks that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there's any need for re-examination, Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, you spoke of a family in Spicasta -- in the sharp rock, Spicasta Stijena, that was killed. That was the Parla family. That family lived on which side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the witness has indicated that he didn't know anything about the confrontation lines, so this is a question which suggests that he would have knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm guided by your comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then rephrase the question or put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were a member of the service of the defenders. Your work as a member of the service was to pick up the bodies and bury them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What defence do you mean? Member of the defence? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were a member of the service of the defenders.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Service. I serviced them. I was not a member. I was a manager of the service working for the army. We had to do that. There was no choice. I had to bury the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So your service was to bury the dead?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that from April 1992 until the Dayton Accord, you buried three and a half thousand soldiers. How were you able to calculate or to come to this approximation?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's the number. There's the ordinal number in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it you mean you went through your notebook and tallied them up.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the document which was shown to you just now, the first column at the left, could you tell us what that column represents?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Even I don't know. What is this? It doesn't seem to be in order. I really don't know. This is as much information as I could obtain for each burial. As for what was put here in front, I really don't know. In my notebook, it goes 1, 2, 3, onwards, in order. So I don't know. Who gave you this? Where did this come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was received by the Defence from the Prosecution. All I can do is give my learned friends a copy of the floppy disk. Maybe we can tender that into evidence so that there should be no dispute as to the source of the document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there's a different problem, whether anything has been added to the documentation given by the witness to who finally transferred it to the Prosecution team. I think that's the problem. It's not a problem whether -- for the time being, I accept that you have the same data on the disks. So I don't think that this would be a good idea at this moment, but please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is indeed not a problem. It will become clear as to the contents of that floppy disk when the evidence unfolds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll wait and see, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, you supplied certain names and information, but this particular document, you did not prepare this yourself?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document? This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That one in your hands, yes.

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My staff member did it. He copied it out from the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to clarify a point. The witness said that whatever he noted down in his notebook was copied onto the floppy disk and that he gave the floppy disk to the police. I think there's no dispute over that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing is what happened afterwards with the data on this floppy disk, and as far as I understand, the Prosecution will present the evidence at a later stage of what exactly happened to this data as they have been provided for by Mr. Sehbajraktarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just clarify one thing, Mr. Sehbajraktarevic? Did you give a floppy disk to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. And everything is just like this in the notebooks, except I'm confused by this first number, which seems to be topsy-turvy. Why it's like that, I really don't know. This first number. Everything else is the same as it is in my notebook. We have those notebooks. It's easy for me to bring them, and we can check things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, how do you define a soldier, or a combatant?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any definitions. After the war in Sarajevo, there's no definition of "soldiers." In the old days, the front was far away from a city. Until this war, I never saw dead [as interpreted] people in town. So there's no definition any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you use to define soldiers or combatants for your records?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used this certificate - I said that a moment ago - brought either by his commander or member of the family, that he was a member of the Territorial Defence or a brigade that was subsequently formed. And I have that also in my company in safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For the transcript, in line 38, 1, it says: "I never saw dead people in town." I think that the interpreter said "these people." At least as it shows on the screen written "D-E-A-D" must be a mistake, that's for sure. But it's "that" or "these," I do not know, but D-E-A-D seems to me to be a mistake. Yes. Mr. Stamp we are now at 10.32 or 3. How much time do you think the re-examination will still take? If it's just a matter of one or two minutes, I think we could proceed. If not, we can find a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that we take this time as a break, because perhaps I might want to confer a bit. So if this time would be convenient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then we will now have a break until 11.00. So we will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before resuming the re-examination of the witness, I have two issues to deal with, but Mr. Ierace, there is something you want to bring to the attention of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could respond very briefly but I think completely, at this stage, if you wish it, in relation to the issue raised by Mr. Piletta-Zanin this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: One of the witnesses the Prosecution will call next week is a journalist by the surname of van Lynden. He arrived at the Tribunal, in preparation to give his evidence, on the 15th -- I'm sorry, the 16th of January, that is three days ago. He brought with him a videotape which contains a segment that runs for approximately two minutes of a shelling of an apartment building in Sarajevo. It was shot on the 5th of December, 1992. Most of that -- those two minutes, are included in the video that was used during my opening. A copy of the video was provided to the Defence yesterday morning, together with a letter saying that the Prosecution proposes to tender that videotape. Last night, we provided a translation of the words spoken by the witness on the tape, that is, words spoken by him in the context of him being a journalist. In other words, in my submission, there could be no reasonable complaint by the Defence as to the timing of the provision of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many pages are provided in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: One page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One page. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, any observation further than what you made this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, but I will mention them later, after we have continued with the cross-examination. I intend to continue and carry on with the case that I have formulated. I will provide you with an explanation at a slightly later hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- we do understand from the Prosecution, we don't want to spend much time on it, that it's just about one page and it's just about words of a journalist that is on a tape which has been provided to you recently but only came into the possession of the Prosecution also recently. What I'd like to know from you at this stage, not in general terms, whether this one page will cause you any problems in preparing for the examination of the witness for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. It will present the same problems, Your Honour. It's a matter of principle, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. And we are constantly aware of the principle matters. On the other hand, we also would like to solve problems, so if you say that there is a problem in the -- in providing translations to the Defence, I fully agree with you, and if this would have been a substantial number of pages, and if the content would have been such that without a translation, could you not have properly -- you could not properly prepare the examination of the witness, I can tell you that in this Chamber we had already the feeling that we should tell the Prosecution that they could not call the witness on short notice, because that would be unfair. On the other hand, if it's just one page, and when you have got one week to prepare for the examination, this Chamber feels that, although we are aware of the principal matter in the background, that this, at this moment, is not a problem where we should interfere and that the Prosecution may proceed. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to persist with regard to this matter. It will take me time to explain this in detail. I'm sorry. If you want me to do so now, I will do so, but I think it will be more useful to do it after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we'll first now complete the examination of the witness, and then immediately afterwards you'll have the opportunity to explain in further detail what your objections are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another issue, and I'm directing myself to both the parties. We've been looking to the exhibits which will be tendered into evidence, and since I heard no objections, I expect that it will be admitted in evidence. That's the list that has been shown to the witness. And especially the status of the persons that were buried seems of importance to the Chamber, and therefore I would like to invite the parties to compromise on how many entries on the whole list were "Cs" and how many entries were "Bs." I think it's a database which can be easily sorted on the column status. So I think it would take you, I think, five to ten minutes to find out. I think that if the parties could agree on the numbers, then this would be an easier way to deal with it. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
