utterances.text: If it please you, Mr. President, I would agree that it would be a very easy way to deal with that one sheet, one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have got -- if it's a database, it's just a matter of sorting on the column of status, and then you'll find that the first, let's say, 300 pages will be "Bs," because that -- no. Yes, "Bs" first and then "Cs" for civilians. I think it's not very difficult, unless it's not a total database, but if it's split up in many small databases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It forms part of a huge batch of databases which will be analysed in evidence which the Prosecution intends to tender before the Court at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So finally, we will be informed about the total number of "Bs" and the total number of "Cs" on the database as it has been provided by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's exactly what the Chamber would like to be informed about. But if you'll present it anyhow, then there's no reason at this moment to invite you to do it in a different way as you intend to do it. Then -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we could proceed with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, we can proceed. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in Mr. Sehbajraktarevic. You can hear us, Mr. Sehbajraktarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Stamp, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will proceed by thanking the witness for attending and testifying on our behalf and indicating to the Court that I have no further questions in re-examination, if it pleases you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This means that we are already at the end of your examination, Mr. Sehbajraktarevic. The Prosecution wanted to confer during the pause whether they had any additional questions or not, and it now turns out that they have no additional questions to be put to you. Any of the colleagues, any further questions? Yes. There's a question from Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. The last column of the report refers to the place of burial. It's the same place always. Could that explain the problem of the numbers? What I mean is that probably the database was sorted out according to the place of burial, and that's why the numbers are not consecutive numbers. What do you think about it?

utterances.speaker: FUAD SEHBAJRAKTAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking about that just a moment ago. It was probably in alphabetical order, this column here, of people buried. This is a list from Kobilja Glava. Everything else is specific: Kobilja Glava, Podastrovi [phoen], Umcate [phoen], Alifakovac. It depended on the location of the cemetery. And if it went in alphabetical order, this must have been -- the order must have been disrupted somehow. That's the only possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no more questions from the Bench, I would like to thank you, Mr. Sehbajraktarevic, for coming a far way from Sarajevo and I would like to thank you for all the information you've given to this Chamber in its efforts to find the truth. Thank you very much for coming, and come home safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Defence, having referred to a document and asked that it be received into evidence, that request we have not objected to. Neither has the Defence raised any issue in respect of the authenticity of that document, and they specifically referred to the source of that document and stated that it was one page from that source, being a compact disk which was delivered to them by the Prosecution and which is on the list of evidence. In those circumstances, I respectfully tender the compact disk with all of the data from which the Defence has taken one page and ask that it be received into evidence. I don't think, having regard to what happened and what the Defence said in cross-examination, that they are objecting to the authenticity of the contents of the disk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps let's first -- before we give a decision on that, let's first try to clarify on this issue what the position of the Defence is, because some questions were put to the witness which indicated that the Defence would like to know for sure that the disk would contain the same data as provided by the witness when he gave his disk to the -- to other persons. Is there any question at this moment, Ms. Pilipovic, about the Defence taking the position that this is not a correct copy of what has been provided in Sarajevo by the witness to a third party?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness first told us that he didn't know on the left side -- what sort of numbers there were on the left side. He doesn't know anything about those numbers. He also said that as far as he knew, that in his memory he had recorded the cause of death. He showed us that in this document, that this has not been entered in this document. So the Defence is questioning the authenticity of this document which is on the floppy disk in respect of the document that is the original, that is the book that the -- I'm referring to the book that the witness has. So the counsel suggests that the witness provides the original notebook to the Prosecution or to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Trial Chamber, if the Trial Chamber so decides. This is the counsel's proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a proposal. I do understand your proposal, but the question now is what is tendered into evidence, because you are tendering one page, one hard-copy page, of the disk, and the Prosecution now tenders into evidence the whole disk.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, counsel has presented this one page to the witness in order to obtain testimony from the witness as to whether this one page demonstrates whether this information, this data, in this document, is authentic and corresponds to what he has noted in his notebook. Today, the witness told me that he doesn't know about these numbers on the side, in the margin, as his numbers were in sequence, as is usual. And he told us that in his notebook, he kept records and entered data on the basis of the doctor's conclusions, obtained from the coroner - he provided his name - and on that basis he entered the cause of death. That was in response to counsel's question as to whether, and on what basis, they entered the cause of death. He said that it hadn't been listed here, hadn't been entered in this document, but it existed in his notebook. Counsel has taken this document -- from that floppy disk in order to verify whether that disk is -- corresponds to the original notebook. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision of the Chamber is that the hard copy of the one page presented by the Defence will be admitted into evidence as D28. I thought it was D28 -- 27. I'm mistaken, D27. And the Prosecution has not yet prenumbered the disk, which it tenders into evidence and which the Chamber decides will also be admitted into evidence. At least since we have some problems about the authenticity, both of disk and therefore of the hard copy made of this one page, it is admitted into evidence and we will hear about it later, as far as I understand. A copy has been provided already to the Defence. So we should then -- we don't have -- we don't need to have copies for the Bench at this moment to look at, but, please, would you number the exhibit and give it to the usher, who will then give it to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The number I think is 3 -- P3630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the number on the disk itself or just on the box?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it pleases Your Honour, this is the number, the exhibit number, I am informed. It is correct identification exhibit number, P3630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see you're looking to the box. Is the number also on the disk?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, on the disk as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you'll have the opportunity to explain further your objections against the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone is on now. I'm not sure whether one can hear me. Thank you, Your Honour. The reason for which counsel must raise the question that it mentioned a short while ago is as follows. The hearings to come are in question in the very near future, the hearing of a witness van Lynden, who is on number 9 in the list provided by the Prosecution, which is a schedule for the appearance of this witness. As I said, he is under number 9, immediately followed by witness under letter "B", for whom we have estimated a time of one and a half hours for the examination-in-chief. We could think that -- we might think that the witness Aernout van Lynden will be heard at the beginning of the week. I think this is correct. There may be some changes but this is the last information I had. Your Honour, there is an essential rule that we have to respect, and that is to permit the accused to allow -- to be able to allow what is being objected to him. This is not the first time. I'm not competent in statistics, but I think that on several occasions, the Prosecution provided counsel with documents in extremis, and I mean by that a few hours or even a few minutes before the hearing, if not at the very beginning of the hearing. They say that it's only one page, that only one page is in question. That's true. But it's a page that was provided on Friday evening when I wasn't there to prepare meetings with members of the Defence counsel, with regard to a hearing that was to take place very soon, at the beginning of next week. The first -- that's the first thing. The second thing - and this is a point I want to insist on, Your Honour - the elements referred to, this cassette, these are elements and this cassette itself, dates back to 1980 -- 1992. van Lynden, the witness van Lynden, was heard, was questioned by the accusation in September or October, I don't have the exact date, perhaps in September, but it doesn't matter, of last year, so we had the time to provide counsel with these translations, and I mean in Serbian, in order to provide Galic, General Galic, with it. I have the Serbian version here in front of me. As far as the written statement is concerned, this witness's written statement, the written statement of Aernout van Lynden, this is, I think, a very important document. It was provided by the Prosecution only a few days ago, on the 11th of January of this year. And, Your Honour, this time limit is just not acceptable. Would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of January, at 1330 hours, I checked with the parties whether they had available everything they needed in respect of witness number 10, they said you had not yet prepared, but on the other witnesses, there were no problems. So I must say that both parties can be blamed for it, you for not reporting that it was not there in time and the Prosecution for not providing you in time with the copies in B/C/S. What I intended to do on the 10th of January, is in order to prevent any waste of time in this courtroom with these kind of problems -- of course, I'm quite prepared to listen to -- this Chamber is prepared to listen to serious problems, but at the same time, we went through the whole list of witnesses. The parties were invited to do similar at the beginning of each week, and so apart from this one page about the video that has been provided to the Prosecution only recently, as far as I understand, so it's not related to whatever the witness has given us in a statement in September or October, so apart from that, I have indicated that I don't want any waste of time on this, and I see that both the Prosecution, as far as I understand, if it's correct what they're saying, and that's what I assume for this moment, and the Defence, have failed to inform this Chamber in time that there were problems as far as the disclosure of B/C/S translations of these statements were. So once again -- I'm talking about statements, not about the video. Once again, the parties have to sit together, and the parties, as they were instructed by the Senior Legal Officer, have to look, at least one week in advance, and see whether they've got everything, and if not, report immediately to the Chamber, or take care that it will be immediately disclosed. But I'm not going to spend any more time on objections raised in respect of these kind of statements if it has not been duly in time before the examination of the witnesses, after the parties have conferred about the disclosure, I'm not going to listen to any complaints in general terms. It's up to you to report immediately to the Chamber if there is any failure to disclose or to disclose in a proper language. Then you can explain to the Chamber and we'll give orders, but we are not going to waste time on it just prior to the calling of the witness. So it may be quite clear to you that statements in general, at the beginning of the week, one week in advance, you can complain and we'll give orders. We will not do that just a few minutes or one witness before the witness to be called in relation to whom this statement should have been disclosed. So please proceed. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I've been thinking of this meeting on the 10th. When we said that there was no problem, there were no problems, I didn't have -- I haven't had the time to verify it. We were referring to the list that I have in front of me and we were talking about documents that would be tendered as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... checked it in the transcript, and we have been talking also about the previous statements given to the Prosecution, and you indicated quite clearly, for example, with the tenth witness, that you had not yet prepared. And so therefore, since there were no observations as far as the ninth witness on the list - and that was Mr. van Lynden - was concerned, this Chamber assumed that there were no problems. If there would have been problems and if you would have not been aware at that very moment, you could have reported that at the next court hearing and not wait for another four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm doing it now, I'm doing it now. I'm reading item 9 on the witness, van Lynden, where it says that there would not be any exhibits. And I think that, if I've understood this well, at the moment we have a document that is going to be tendered as an exhibit. I think I've understood this clearly. So if there are going to be exhibits that will be presented in extremis, counsel will not accept them. It's not possible for this Defence counsel to be treated in such a manner, such a vulgar manner, and to have some documents submitted to us a few hours before a hearing which we have never spoken about before, in the sense of exhibits. So this is the point that I wanted to make, Your Honour. I don't know if your Trial Chamber will tolerate such things, but the counsel is quite surprised by the fact that a few hours before the hearing they are presented with cassettes and a text, although it is fully aware of the fact that it is not possible to confer with General Galic, on one hand, because I would be absent, and because General Galic would not have access to this text. So in application of all the legal provisions which are applicable, we demand that this be rejected, in quite clear terms. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If the Prosecution got into its possession only recently the tape, that creates a situation which cannot generally be foreseen. If there's any need, in time, to better prepare, you of course can apply for it, and the time you need, of course, is related, as far as this Chamber can accept, is related to the kind of document, the length of the document, the contents of the document, whether it's very technical, whether it's legal, whether it's... So it all depends. Of course, you can apply for a further period of time in which you can prepare and discuss with your client the content of the tape, and we'll find a solution for that. I don't think that if you receive such a tape on short notice as Prosecution, I don't think that the word "vulgar" would be appropriate. Mr. Ierace, would you make any additional observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Firstly, my learned friend mentioned that van Lynden will follow immediately on Witness B. That is incorrect. He was advised by correspondence yesterday that there is a change to the order of the witnesses and Witness B is now to be followed by Witness D and then by van Lynden. In other words, Mr. van Lynden is not likely to be called until Tuesday, at the earliest. Secondly, I'm concerned about the Trial Chamber may think that the statement of Mr. van Lynden has been disclosed late. The statement is dated the 10th of October, 2001. The English version was given to the Defence on the 26th of October, 2001. The B/C/S version was given to the Defence on the 26th of November, 2001. This tape is approximately two minutes long. Except for two scenes, it is identical to a tape shown during the opening. The rough translation, which was provided to the Defence, was provided the day after we received it, and therefore, Mr. President, in my respectful submission, there is simply no basis, no reasonable basis, for complaint. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how much time would you need to prepare -- to discuss the content of the video? You have seen it meanwhile or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you mean with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have seen it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you need? I think General Galic has the opportunity to look at the video in the detention facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To watch it at the same time as anyone else, he would need two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you still need to discuss the content? You have got an idea now of what it is about. The Chamber has not -- apart from that, that part of it would be the same as in the introductory video. How much time would you need to discuss the matter with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for this question, but I still have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is, I don't know. I can't know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at this moment, since you give us no further information, there's no reason for us at this moment to change the order of witnesses, as suggested by the Prosecution. Just let us know when you are short of time in preparing the examination of Mr. van Lynden because of the late transmission of -- late disclosure of this video to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that this will probably be the case. This is quite probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll hear from you. Then I think the next witness will be heard in closed session. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But Ms. Pilipovic, you would first like to make an observation. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should just like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence has not been informed that there has been a change in the order of hearing the testimony of the witnesses. That is to say, that Witness D will be heard before van Lynden. I'd like to ask my learned friends when they advised me of this. All I was informed of was that Witness B, Mesud Jusufovic, will not -- that Mesud Jusufovic be heard, but Witness B, who we're going to have next. I have no information as to the change in order for Witness D.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, a letter was placed in the Defence box I think at about 6.30 last night, that is, the Defence box for Ms. Pilipovic, which sets out the change in the order of the witnesses and also indicates the next two witnesses to be called, following on the list which had previously been provided. It also contains the exhibit numbers in relation to those two additional witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you think you provided yesterday to the Defence. Has the Registry been informed about it? Has the Chamber been informed about it? I didn't find anything in my letter box, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We propose to provide that after court this morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll understand that if this issue is raised by the Defence, that the Court would be very much pleased to be provided with similar information, so that at least we know what it's all about, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I have copies available if you'd like them at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll read them later on, and I think we'll continue now. Ms. Pilipovic, you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, last night -- thank you, Your Honour. I was informed last night that some documents were placed in my locker. I picked them up at 8.15 this morning, but I have not given a receipt to my friends. In the material there are 23 pages of translation, of statements taken in the district court in Paris from two witnesses that my colleagues would like to introduce via Mr. van Lynden, as a witness. In this folder, I just have the receipt, but it does not say -- I haven't got the letter that informs me of the change of order. It states here on the list that I am being given 23 pages, which I picked up this morning. The Trial Chamber can take a look at this. Those are the documents which the Prosecution wishes to introduce via the next witness, van Lynden. But I have not received information as to the change of order. So that was the problem that my colleague and I wish to raise, and the Defence finds it difficult to understand this kind of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please take a position as far as 23 pages are concerned instead of one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I can tell you that my case manager delivered the letter personally to Ms. Pilipovic's box immediately after I signed it, and then at about 6.30 she rang, personally, Ms. Pilipovic and told her that the correspondence was -- that there was correspondence in her box for her. I, of course, don't doubt what Ms. Pilipovic says to the Trial Chamber, that she has not located that letter, but it was nevertheless placed in her box. In any event, we will of course, immediately after court, provide her with a photocopy of a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But one of the other issues, and perhaps a more important one at this moment, is the 23 pages she has been provided with, at least she found in her letter box.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think my friend is under a misunderstanding that the other documents - that is, the 23rd pages - relate to Mr. van Lynden. They do not. That is simply material which is being provided as part of our ongoing obligations in relation to disclosure. I'll seek some more information in relation to those 23 pages, but at this stage I can certainly assure the Chamber they bear no relationship to witnesses being called next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is there any clear indication as to -- that they relate to the testimony of Mr. van Lynden or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this document, it says that it is -- that it is the transcript of the 5th of December, 1992, where it says "Lynden." The number is 2, and then numbers 3 and 4. They are, in fact, two statements taken in the district court in Paris, and from this document one can conclude that these two statements, which the Defence is looking at for the first time today, are, in fact, an attempt to introduce this through van Lynden. Nothing on the documents states that they are documents which are being especially handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask both parties to inform this Chamber on whether these 23 pages will be used somewhere in the next one or two weeks or not. If not, we are just dealing at the moment with the one page. If so, we will further consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can assure you that they have nothing to do with Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear enough an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I can now understand why my friends were so concerned. Clearly there has been a misunderstanding. Clearly they thought they were receiving 23 pages which related to the witness following the one about to be called. I can assure them that they misread the letter and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it related to the witness which will be called next week, the 23 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then I'll just leave to sort this out to the parties during their at least weekly meeting where they will check whether they have everything they need in order to be prepared for the examination of witnesses. And I think -- Ms. Pilipovic, you're still standing. Is there any other observation you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I am surprised that my colleagues have changed the order of the witnesses, because for Witness D, the document that they wished to introduce through Witness D, they sent me those documents just a few days ago. I think we must respect our agreements and that the deadline be seven days before the appearance of the witness in court. That is why I am surprised with this change in the order of witnesses. I would appeal to you to ensure that the Defence is informed at least a week beforehand of the witnesses and material to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to Witness D, a letter was provided to the Prosecution [sic], I think early this week or late last week, informing them that the Prosecution proposed to tender through that witness a video clip which takes approximately 30 seconds, which appeared in the opening video segment. In other words, that was added to the exhibit list. That was the only change to the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, let's just try to be very practical. Has the recently provided material to the Defence, was it one week in advance of the hearing of Witness D?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll check the date of the letter. I think it was, but I'll check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there has been a change in the representation of the case manager at the Bar table over the week. It might save time if I give you that date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll hear from that later, and one week is the absolute minimum. When will the parties sit together again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There has been no meeting organised between us, but especially in light of what's occurred this morning, this misunderstanding, I'll speak to my friends at the next break and arrange for us to have a meeting later on this afternoon, if they are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was the last meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There hasn't been a meeting, I think, for about two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's exactly against what this Chamber expects the parties to do. We are not going to spend any more time on you just ignoring of what the Chamber has said. So you have to communicate far better. I'm not saying who is responsible for that, but this Chamber expects the parties to behave professionally in such a way that at least every week, one week in advance, it has been checked. We arranged for a meeting together with the Senior Legal Officer of this Chamber, and I now, to my disappointment, have to find out that it's not taken as seriously as we intended you to take it. Ms. Pilipovic, if there is anything new and substantive to add, please proceed. Otherwise, I would like to continue the examination of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The essential point is that our trial began on the 9th. I came to the Hague on the 7th and informed my colleagues that I would like to have a meeting with them. And I repeat this, I reiterate this. So far, I have received no proposals for an upcoming meeting from my colleagues. And as regards our professional work, I think we ought to respect your proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber wants to be informed at the beginning of each week when the last meeting took place and whether there are any problems or not. That's the ruling of this Chamber. And we'll see how that works. Mr. Ierace, if there is something substantive you would like to add, go ahead. If not, we would like to proceed with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President, following that request, I met with Mrs. Pilipovic two days running. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this issue - and as you may have noticed a bit of irritation on all sides - has been dealt with, I would say, enough at this moment. Let's not look back. Let's look forward and see whether we can -- everyone in this courtroom, we included, can perform better. The Prosecution may call its next witness. But I think it will be in closed session, if that's correct. We are quite sure about that so we don't close the curtains and pull them up again later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: It's not in closed session. It's actually protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Protective measures, yes. Then, Mr. Usher, will you please close the curtains and put everything in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not at this moment the exact decision on the protective measures. Could it -- we ask to bring it to us, but if the parties agree what exactly the protective measures are that are granted for the witness, please inform us and see whether the parties agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply face and voice distortion, as well as pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, do you have any --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Are you requesting the voice distortion as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are not aware of that at all. If you request voice distortion, we need to be informed 24 hours in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's all right. We can keep the face distortion without the voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it, of course, depends on what has been requested and what the order has been. Do you have the copy of the decision at this moment available to you? Because I want to verify that we are making no mistakes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take advantage of the pause to indicate to the Chamber that there were telephone meetings between the Defence and the Prosecution when we asked that all important documents should be communicated to us by fax so that there should be no mistake. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have a copy of the letter in the meantime, the letter that we should have received yesterday evening at 6.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think this could be sorted out outside of this courtroom. Did we find the order?

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the delay. We are just trying to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's convenient for the Court, we might suggest that we take the break now as opposed to later so we can sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is all right as far as the interpreters' booth is concerned and the technical people, but if there are no objections, I would then suggest that we have a break until 12.20 and then continue until quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No objections from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are objections from the interpreters, so we cannot follow your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't listen well. There were no objections from the interpreters' booth, so we will then adjourn Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. until 12.20. --- Break taken at 12.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Kalra.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I apologise for the delay. We have located both the Prosecution motion as well as the decision given by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution's motion was dated 30th of October, 2001, and in that we requested, for Witness B, expunging names and identifying information from the Tribunal's public records, non-disclosure to the public of any records identifying the victim, giving of testimony through image or voice-altering devices or closed-circuit television, and assignment of pseudonym. The decision was an oral decision on the 6th of November [sic], 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to read. We are talking about Witness B. When I read the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, if I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: I've actually spoken to the witness during the break. We've been having ongoing discussions where she has been considering removing the protective measures. When I spoke to her just recently, she would like to have those protective measures removed completely and testify in open session, if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I think the public character of the trial is of major importance, but it's the second time this week that after we put the curtains down, we have to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think the public character of the trial is far more important than the extra work for the usher. But please, Mr. Usher, would you remove all the protective measures again. Yes, please. By the way, as far as I read the request, it says Witness B requests pseudonym, face, and voice alteration. So that's, I think, not -- that has been granted. Yes. There must be a mistake in the record, in the transcript, because it says the 6th of November. But of course, it's the 6th of December, exactly at seven minutes past 2.00 in the afternoon, that the decision was given by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not your fault. It's the fault of the ... Yes, please. You may bring in the witness, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This Court understood that although you had been introduced initially to testify under a pseudonym, which would have been "Witness B," you finally decided that you will testify in open court and that no protective measures were needed. So that's the reason why I'll call you just by your name and not "Witness B." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So Ms. Zaimovic - I understand you are Ms. Zaimovic - for your testimony, you are required by the Rules to give a solemn declaration, and the text will be given to you by the usher. Would you then please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. It is now a member of the Prosecution's team who will examine you as a witness. Ms. Kalra, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Can you please state your name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Fatima Zaimovic. I was born on the 20th of January, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Are you the head nurse at Kosevo Hospital children's surgery?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: How long have you been in that position?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have been in that position for 33 years. You mean as head nurse?

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Yes, as head nurse, yes.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: As head nurse, I have been head nurse since 1979.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you work in this capacity throughout the period between September 1992 and August 1994?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: How many nurses were working in your department during this time?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: When the war started, there were about 35 nurses in the hospital. However, at the very beginning, more than ten nurses left, so that about 24 or 25 nurses remained. I can't remember the exact number. And then the last convoy that left Sarajevo took another ten nurses with it, these nurses being of different ethnicity, but the first ten that left were Serbs, who left the clinic without even saying goodbye, which was quite unusual for the atmosphere that prevailed at our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: How many nurses were actually working during the war, after the nurses had left?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: After the nurses had left, about 15 were left, and so we started working at the hospital with these 15 nurses, which was difficult, as nurses came from different parts of the city, and due to shelling, very often they did not come to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: How were your responsibilities as head nurse different during the war as opposed to before the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: My duties were more or less the same, but the volume of work, much of which was done by my assistants before, and I supervised them, I had to take over because there weren't enough of us to carry out all those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about the conditions at Kosevo Hospital, particularly within your department. Did you have electricity during the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you have running water?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: We had medicines. We had something in reserve, which is normal for all hospitals in the world. They have to have a pharmacy and some in stock. And then the Doctors Without Frontiers came and they assisted with the medicines, and UNICEF was there too to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: How did these shortages affect the running of your department?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult. We were scared. I have to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did your department treat both military and civilian patients?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: At my department, only children were treated, and of course they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: What age group did you treat?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: At my clinic, before the war and during the war and now, we have patients from birth up to 14 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Was Kosevo Hospital ever shelled or sniped at between September of 1992 and August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you remember how often this happened?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I know for certain that there were a large number of shells, and especially sniper bullets or whatever they call them, those very large bullets that could go through walls and cause real disaster.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Was there any military equipment in the hospital, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any -- if there was any military equipment in the area surrounding the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: How did the children react to the shelling and sniping of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Their reaction was terrible. The children panicked, started screaming, and it was very difficult to calm them down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: What if any precautions did you take to protect the children within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: We were not ready for the war, so we had no preparations for it. What we did have at the clinic were long corridors. The building was built in Austrian times and the basements were not equipped for accommodation, so it was very hard. The patients who were bedridden were kept in the corridors, and attended by nurses. And then the small children that we could carry, we would take to the basement, which, as I said, had no facility. It was horrible. It was really difficult. They were screaming and crying, afraid to be left alone, and hanging on to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Were any patients or staff members injured by shells or sniper fire within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two of my colleagues were wounded -- no, killed, at work, because a shell hit their room. It was a direct hit. I don't remember the date. I know it was cold, very cold. It was in wintertime. I came to work in the morning and found those two good colleagues of mine, who were dead. One had two small children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Can you recall what year that took place in?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993. Also, in 1993, a wonderful lady, an engineer, was killed, who helped us a lot in improvising the premises, to put the children there, so that we could move from the traumatology department to Dip, where she had her office. On her way to her office, a shell fell and killed her on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you recall when that took place?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: This occurred in 1993, around the middle of the year. I think so, but please don't hold me to the dates because I really didn't keep track of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about the children that you were treating. Can you tell us approximately the number of children that would come in to your department on an average day?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It varied. Sometimes we had two to three. Sometimes children came in groups, when there was very heavy shelling. And there were times when there would be ten or six or seven children coming, and they were so frightened, covered in blood, mud, dismembered. Their parents would be crying. The staff would be crying. The walls would start crying, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: That number of two to three children per day, did that continue consistently throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Two to three years. But I remember one heavy shelling at a school at Otoka, in Nemanjina Street, in Vase Miskina Street, and on those occasion we had a very large number of patients. The worst occasion was when the school was hit. That was on the 9th of November. And the Otoka shelling was on the 10th of November. We hadn't even recovered from the children at school, and the next day, 11 children came from Otoka. Two were dead and the others were mostly brothers and sisters, as they were all hiding in a passageway. The weather was fine and the children wanted to go outside, and a shell fell and wounded them very, very seriously. Believe me, they didn't choose the time or place or day. They opened fire at will. They would fall silent for a day or two, then the children would feel more relaxed, go out into the streets, and then they would open fire and kill those innocent children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: You mentioned a few incidents there. The incident on the 9th of November, do you remember which year that was?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Does it follow that the incident on the 10th of November also took place in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993. Both the 9th and the 10th. All this was in 1993. That year was very hard for us. We had no electricity or gas or water. Water was brought in truck tanks. The food was running out. It was really hard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you personally treat the children in the incidents that you just spoke of on the 9th and 10th of November?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Together with a team of other nurses, we would admit them to the department. Then a team of surgeons, together with the anaesthesiologist, would come to assess which child needed to be operated first, who was most at risk, and then they would be operating day and night and then brought back to the ward. Everything - treatment, infusions, keeping the children quiet - all this had to be done and taken care of by us, those of us working in the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you remember what types of injuries those children suffered from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Each child had two or three wounds. The shells were dreadful. Some were left without legs or arms. Some children were so badly hurt by -- one child had his kidney and liver and spleen destroyed by shrapnel, or a blood vessel would be hit and we couldn't stop the haemorrhaging, so that they would pass away. So on an average, each child had two or three injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific incidents that occurred on the 10th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was at Otoka, on the 10th of October --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: -- the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence objects to the manner in which the question has been put to the witness, as the witness said, in answer to an earlier question: "Please don't insist on the dates. Don't hold me to the dates I give."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was, I think, on a specific question, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my learned friend rephrase her question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're doing so. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Are there any incidents that you recall that took place in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a number of them. In 1992, in the autumn, yes, a child, a wonderful child, was injured, in Jelena Vitas Street. I remember that extremely well. His name was Dario Vapetic. He has stuck in my memory. His parents, with their neighbours, wanted to light a fire, and they collected some paper in the yard of the building, which was fully surrounded. And when they were about to do that, a shell fell in the yard, and in a single moment, that boy lost his mother and father and both grandparents. You can't imagine. A lot of children came. The adults were treated in the other departments and we treated the children. When he arrived, he was out of his mind. He kept repeating, "Auntie, Auntie, I saw my dad's head flying through the air." It took us a lot of time to calm him down. And I don't know whether that child is still suffering from the consequences. I'm not in touch with him. As days passed, he started -- he was incontinent in bed, and then a grandmother came one day and she took him away. As he was leaving -- we had become very close and we loved each other, and he wrote down -- they called me Tina. And he said, "Auntie Tina, I love you so much that I simply don't want to leave you." And he drew a vase - he was only 6 years old - and a flower in that vase, on an old piece of paper, and I treasure this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you recall which injury he specifically --

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't badly hurt. He had a large number of wounds, but they were not life-threatening. And they were treated quite quickly. He was lucky.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately which month within the autumn of 1992 that took place?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, 1992. I remember that very well, because I think of that little boy often.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Where were you living during the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was living close to the hospital. The district is called Breka. It's right behind the hospital. So that my coming to the hospital was dangerous, but not as much as it was for the other nurses who lived in Dobrinja or at Alipasino Polje or at Hrasno, and so on. So that because of the proximity of my home and everything else, I went to the clinic every day and stayed from morning till night, and very often I stayed overnight when other nurses did not manage to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: What part of Sarajevo could you see from your home?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Breka is on an elevation above town, so I could see a part of Mount Trebevic and a part of the town, and I could even see those two large UNIS skyscrapers that were very badly shelled. All this can be seen from my window.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you ever see any activity that took place on Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I saw a gun behind a rock. This area is known as Osmice. All the people of Sarajevo know what that means. It's a big rock behind which a gun was hidden, and it would come out and open fire on the town. One morning - it was summer. The weather was very fine - I got up early and I sat on the balcony, when I heard a terrible explosion. People had filled barrels with explosive material and pushed them down the hill, which simply destroyed some homes as they hit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you remember when you saw the incident of the barrels?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I can't remember the date. Indeed, I am so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you remember the year in which that took place?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. This must have been towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, when the shooting was fiercest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw a gun coming out on Mount Trebevic. Could you see whether that gun had wheels?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just saw the barrel. It's not a gun. It's a tank. I know it's a tank, and it had a gun which you would see and a shell coming out of it, hitting the houses. These were all private homes on that part of the slopes. There are no apartment buildings, only private family homes. Anyone living in Sarajevo knows about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: And when did you see the tank coming out on to Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He was there all the time. It was there all the time, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Does that include the period between September 1992 and August 1994?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Were you ever sniped at during the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the war. My husband and I started off to work in the morning, and a sniper targeted us and the bullet whizzed past my hair, singeing this front portion. I ducked down and it whizzed past my husband's neck. Luckily, we weren't hit. And we were very frightened, and we decided never to go to work together from then on, because we thought that as we had two children, if either one of us was killed, at least that would leave one of us alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you recall what month that took place in?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: The weather was very fine. We didn't dare look at the leaves or look up. We always looked down because we were very afraid of being hit, so we couldn't feel autumn and spring and anything going on around us. We were too busy looking down at our feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Do you recall which year that took place in?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you feel safe when you were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did the children feel safe, to the best of your recollection, while they were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. They quite certainly didn't, because when they heard any shooting - which might have been in town but the echoes reached the Kosevo Hospital - they would jump out of bed, any of the children who were able to, and the children who weren't able to, who were bedridden, they would be extremely scared, and the children who could, rushed to us for protection. They were terribly afraid of the shells and the shooting. And that was probably because they had experienced the wounding, and so when they heard those terrible sounds of shooting and explosions, this had a terrible effect on the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you see any emotional effects in these children that was caused by the shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. Some children withdrew into themselves. Others began wetting their beds, children who had never done that before. And they did many other things which I just can't remember now, because in 1993, we included psychologists and pedagogists working with us at the clinic, with the children, to help them get over the war as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did any staff member show any signs of emotional stress from the shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We are all humans, and we all experience things in different ways, each in our own way. At my own clinic, there were two nurses who had psychological problems, and they are still being treated at psychiatric wards, and actually those two stopped working. One was an assistant nurse and the other one was a technician working in the theatre, operating theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: What emotional effects, if any, did the shelling and sniping of civilians have on you personally?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was terribly afraid. I have to be quite frank in saying that. And when I was on my own, I would realise just how much it had all affected me and just how afraid I was. I was afraid for my family. I was afraid for the injured and wounded children. I was afraid whether I'd be up to the task, up to doing everything the job required. But, you know, those small children, when they smiled and laughed and did a drawing for me or asked me, "Auntie Tina, why are you so sad," I would collect myself and carry on working, doing the best I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Did you ever suffer from any health problems that were related -- that you believe are related to the stress from the war?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, when the ceasefire came into being and there was less shooting at town - although there still was shooting and they would do this in an underhand way and kill in an underhand way - I had a very serious heart attack. Probably it was the culmination of everything that I had experienced. So I had to be absent from the clinic for a time following my heart attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Zaimovic. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kalra. Ms. Zaimovic, questions will be put to you now by Defence counsel from the accused. Ms. Pilipovic, would you please proceed in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zaimovic, good day to you.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You were answering questions put to you by my colleague. What I should now like to ask you is whether on the 9th of April, 2000, you talked to the investigators of the Tribunal and gave a statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date but, yes, probably I did, if it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is what you set out in your statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is, but perhaps not all the details are included in that, because I remember a lot of things as I go along and there are many other -- many more things that I could put in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You worked at the children's ward of Kosevo Hospital since 1978; is that right? Or you were the head nurse?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I became head nurse in 1979. Before that, I had worked as a nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of the medical staff in your ward, in the ward you were head nurse in?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean before the aggression or after the aggression?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you what the ethnic composition was of the medical staff employed in your department, and let me remind you that you said, in response to a question from my learned colleague, when the nurses of Serb ethnicity began to leave. And you said, when the war began.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the war began, they simply left, a part of the nurses. Some of the nurses left and some stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you're referring to Serbian nurses leaving. I don't remember that. Could you please give us the exact line where the witness said that Serbian nurses were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a problem for me now to find the line in question, but Mrs. Zaimovic did state that when the war began there were 35 nurses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: More than ten nurses of Serb ethnicity left?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And among them, of those ten, there were assistant employees, orderlies too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Kalra?

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it assists the Court, the reference is, in the English version, page 66 -- 65, I'm sorry, line 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am able to answer that question. I can answer it if that is required.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you when that was. When I say "when," the year and month, please.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say the fourth -- you said the fourth. Do you mean the fourth month, April?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, April, when the aggression began but when you could still move through town to go to Pale, Foca and the other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have used the word "aggression." Could you clarify that, please -- qualify it?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is the word that we use. And I really do think that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "We use," who do you mean "we"?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the people of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So the word "aggression" for you means what?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You know what an aggression is. When they have guns and snipers in front of the town and they begin killing innocent children and mothers and all the other innocent population of Sarajevo, Madam. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I am well able to understand the emotions you are experiencing, but I think that I am asking questions in a proper manner. You used the word "aggression." Now, on that 4th of April, why did 35 nurses leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that 35 left. I said that ten nurses left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean ten nurses of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that was really what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know why they left?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: They probably knew what was coming, because their entire families were at Pale, in Foca, in Visegrad, and the other places. And there are documents to bear this out. You can check it out for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did something happen before the 4th of April, when, as you say, the war began, and you say that it began on the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know about that. I was in shock for a long time, with all the events that were taking place. I just couldn't believe that it was happening, that anything like that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened on the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was there something characteristic that happened on that day? Because you say the fourth month.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said the fourth month, April, not the 4th of the month. I said that those nurses left in April. Now, what actually happened, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was anything happening in the town itself, in April? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go into town?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went into town. I think that you know what was going on better than me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In April, when you went into town, was there anything unusual compared to the daily rhythm of the town?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. People were -- they were restless and they were buying more than they usually bought, more than they needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Your department, where you were head nurse, how many patients can it take in?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Forty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the director of your hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to state his full name and surname?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about April.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: In April, it was Professor Docent Dr. Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And before Dr. Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: His first man, primarius, Dr. Mirjan Lomas, who stayed with us until the end of the war, and we sent him off nicely when he had to retire, gave him a nice send-off.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us how many nurses left the hospital when the war broke off. Did the doctors leave as well?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many doctors actually left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The doctors who left, you say you don't know how many there were, but do you know what ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: There were Bosniaks and Serbs and Croats. At my clinic, and throughout the war, two Croats remained on the job and three Serbs, and we got on very, very well, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Croats," "Croat nurses," lady nurses, and "Serb nurses," yes, you were referring to nurses, but I asked you about doctors. How many doctors left the hospital? You said that Bosniak and Croat doctors left.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, who left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That means that quite a number of them left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How many Serb and Croat doctors stayed on during the war at your clinic? If you don't know, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't give you a number. It was my job to look after the nurses rather than the doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the head of your department, the children's surgery ward?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Docent Dr. Dizdarevic, who in the meantime became a professor, so he is now Professor Dr. Dizdarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So he was the head of the department and director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He was director of the children's surgical clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the director of Kosevo Hospital as a whole?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was Professor Dr. Faruk Konjuhodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did he become director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was from the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That means that until the end of 1992, who was the hospital director?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the name, but he was a wonderful man, and doctor as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know which ethnic group he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke today about the shelling of Kosevo Hospital. Can you tell us when the hospital was shelled for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from which direction the shells came?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that either, because there were shells coming from all directions. And I'm not a military expert. I can't tell you where the shells came from. We just heard them reverberating, the echoes, the screams, and the cries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us you saw a tank.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from my balcony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see the tank from the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that from your balcony you could see a tank. Where was that tank?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we call that place Osmice, and next to the Osmice there's a large rock, and he was probably taking cover from behind the rock and then he would come out and shoot. But I think that that's common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you see the tank for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your answer, that you can't remember? Can I take it that you don't remember the date?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I can't remember the date. A lot of time has gone by since then, a lot of pain, a great deal of stress, for me to be able to remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether observers, UN observers, came to your hospital? Did they visit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who came, but I do know that foreign journalists would come by very frequently to see how we lived and worked, and that they would usually visit the children's surgical department, bringing sweets and apples to the children, and they made the children happy. Now, whether any soldiers came, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you lived near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What floor was the children's surgical department?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the second floor. My department was on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From your department and the windows of that department, what part of Sarajevo can you best see when you look out of the windows?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: We can hardly see a thing outside the hospital window, because there are large chestnut trees which block the view.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you could see Trebevic from your balcony, could you tell us what Trebevic is?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Trebevic is a mountain above Sarajevo, and it's a good picnic spot, excursion spot. The citizens of Sarajevo would go up there, and I did too, with my children, to spend some time there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the environs of Sarajevo, were there other excursion sites, as you put it? Is it a hill or a mountain?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: A mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are there any other elevations around Sarajevo of that nature?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course there are, yes. You know very well that Sarajevo is built in a valley, surrounded by elevations, and each of these elevations has a name: Bjelasnica, Poljina, Trebevic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Near the hospital and your place of residence, is that where Zuc and Hum hills are located, elevations of that kind?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From your balcony, can you see those hills?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, you can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever climb up those hills, and do you know what is at the top of the hill?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean generally speaking. Did you ever go to the top?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, yes, but never during the war, or after the war either, because I'm afraid of mines and all the residue from the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you went before the war and climbed up those hills, could you see Sarajevo from those elevations?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite remember. We would walk in the forest, breathe in the fresh air. We never thought about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us about the shelling, did you, while you were in the hospital, actually see the hospital being shelled?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion I was actually present, and the second ward for internal medicine is near our own clinic, and the shell directly whizzed into the patient's room. Two patients were killed and another patient was horribly wounded, and we heard terrible screams coming from that ward.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was sometime in 1993. It was a very strong, cold winter. The weather was awful. And all the tinfoil that we had -- and plastic foil that we had set up on the windows was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see the direction where the shell came from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
