utterances.text: No. How could you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the place from which shells were being fired?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Just that one tank. I keep mentioning that tank, the one that I personally saw, and I think everybody else knew that it was there. It was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as for the snipers, did you ever see a sniper shooter?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Can you actually see him?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you. You said that you and your husband were on your way to work when a sniper targeted you.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to judge the direction the sniper fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were so frightened that we never gave any thought to things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What part of town were you in at the time?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was on my way to work, and I was passing by the orthopaedics clinic. I was on the staircase at the entrance to the hospital. I know that for a fact. I know exactly where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you never saw any BH army positions during the war.

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's right; I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know of the existence of the BH army, do you not?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course it existed, but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From your own house to your place of work, on your route, did you ever happen to come across a soldier?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Kalra, you wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: My learned friend did not indicate -- she indicated that Ms. Zaimovic had said that she never saw any BH army positions during the war. My recollection is that she said she did not see any BH army positions near the hospital during the war. If my learned friend could give us a page reference, a line reference, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I began cross-examining the witness, I asked the witness whether she had given a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal, and in my cross-examination, I am using parts of the statement, of what the witness said in the statement, because she said that she did indeed make a statement, which she herself signed. And the Defence therefore considers that in the cross-examination, as this is a Prosecution Exhibit supplied by the Prosecution to the Defence, that we have every right to cross-examine on the facts set out in the statement given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Kalra.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: If my learned friend could give us a reference within the statement, and in future references, when she is conducting her cross-examination, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Pilipovic, that during the last few days we have met this problem now and then, and you were invited -- and of course you're referring to the statement and not to the testimony, so to that extent it's quite clear that you refer to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in order to assist the Chamber to better understand, we invited you always to quote literally that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I only have the B/C/S version of the statement. The page is 03023784. Paragraph 3, I can quote, but I apologise to the interpreters for not having the English version. I don't think I received it. "Throughout the time I worked in the hospital, I never saw any BH army positions in the vicinity of the hospital."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Am I correct, then, that the objection of Ms. Kalra should be sustained? Because you're now saying that the statement contains that she didn't see any BIH positions in the vicinity of the hospital, and when referring to the statement, you made no --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just asked her whether that was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what she said, and she confirmed that it was correct, that she had never seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think you put a question to her whether she had ever seen any BIH positions, and her statement was as you read it now, or -- let me just check on what exactly your question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's at line -- page 86, line 19, if that assists the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I read this line and it says: "In your statement, you said that you never saw any BH army positions during the war." The lines you just read to us are limited to the vicinity of the hospital. So, again, I would appreciate a high degree of precision in confronting a witness with an earlier statement or earlier testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My second question would be whether she had seen them close to the hospital. And that is precisely why I wanted to draw the witness's attention to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, witness, you never saw any soldiers en route from your house to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any soldiers, throughout the war, in that part of town where your apartment is located -- where your home is located and where your institution is located?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your colleagues from Hrasno, Alipasino Polje and Dobrinja would also come to work?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did your colleagues from Dobrinja tell you the route they took to work, how they came to work?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult for them to get to work. They had to run across most of the places. They were very tired and they -- it would take them an hour to recover from their journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Dobrinja yourself?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that Dobrinja for you was as if you were going to France. Could you clarify this answer, please?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It seemed so far because of all those threats, that threatened us from all places, the shells, the bullets, et cetera, so no one had the courage to go out. They would only go out when it was absolutely necessary to do something.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you could see Trebevici and high-rise buildings from your balcony, high-rise buildings in the surroundings. Which buildings are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: They were the two UNIS buildings, skyscrapers - that's what we called them - because when they would shoot in the building -- at these UNIS buildings, you would see these light bullets which were constantly being fired at them. You could see this on television and in reports which the various agencies transmitted at all times. They fired tracer bullets at these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see this personally, you saw it on television?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this personally. I could see that from my balcony.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What did you see personally?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: How the bullets were being fired at this building and how they shattered the windows and how they set the building alight. The building was on fire, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone firing from that building?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. It was impossible to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I think you used approximately half an hour, the same time as the Prosecution used. Could you just indicate how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall make an effort to bring this to -- this examination, this cross-examination, to a conclusion with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the shelling that the children survived, who were in your clinic, in your institution, did you see any of these shellings?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, because we were working in the clinic. They would bring these children to us. I didn't see any of this. When you are confined in the premises of the clinic, you can't see this. You only hear the reverberation, the blast, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about heavy shelling of the school in 1993, November -- on the 9th of November 1993. Did you see this shelling?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. How could I have?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which part of town this school is located?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's in Acipasino Polje, I think it is there -- Alipasino Polje. I'm not sure of the exact location but I think it's there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At a later date, did you hear where the shell came from, or the shell that fell on the school?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, in Sarajevo, did you ever see snipers firing from the UNIS skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: FATIMA ZAIMOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't have seen that from my window and from my building, of course, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Is there any need for re-examination, Ms. Kalra?

utterances.speaker: MS. KALRA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We are concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the colleagues, any further questions? Then, Mrs. Zaimovic, I'd like to thank you for coming this long way to this Court, and of course this Court had noticed that giving the information asked by the parties, of course, brought into your memory, I think, events that made you emotional now and then, and of course we have understanding for the emotions you showed in this courtroom. I'd like to thank you very much for informing this court and we wish you a good journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have got ten minutes left. Does the Prosecution think that it will be of any use to start for these ten minutes? Or it depends on how you -- what issues you have to question about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, not only do I think that we could not make use of that time, in any event we don't have a witness to call at this stage. The next witness will be available on Monday morning. I anticipated that that witness would go to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic, I still want to apologise for breaking into the cross-examination, as far as the leaving of Serbian nurses was concerned. I later found out what caused my confusion. The answer of the witness first was that in the last convoy, nurses of different ethnicity left the hospital, and that was what was still in my mind, and only afterwards she said that the first ten were of Serbian -- so I apologise for breaking in, perhaps in not a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that, at this moment, we should adjourn until next Monday. Madam Registrar, we start at what time next Monday? I think it was at 9.00. Am I correct? Madam Registrar is just checking the Court schedule, which changes now and then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court calendar here says 9.30, but I was informed by my colleagues that we are going to start at 9.00, in Courtroom III, next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there has been a change of courtroom. We will be in Courtroom III next Monday, and if we start at 9.00, would this cause any difficulties for one of the parties? Because if they had on the schedule that we would start at 9.30, travel arrangements might be of importance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, my correction, in this calendar, it says starting at 9.30, so I'm not sure whether we start at 9.00 or 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For reasons related to flight, I would prefer, because that would allow me to be here on Monday. This is just an administrative problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you have to arrive on Monday morning, and therefore ... Yes. So we will then stick to the court schedule, as far as the time is concerned. That's 9.30 next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The courtroom will be Courtroom III?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that's a change. Yes. So we will adjourn to next Monday at 9.30 in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.37 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of January, 2002, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
